```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  txt <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- paste(txt, collapse = "\n")
  txt <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", txt, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(txt, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

summary_data <- fromJSON("colombia_after_independence_summary.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
sett_data <- fromJSON("colombia_after_independence_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("colombia_after_independence_source_ledger.json5")

subregions <- summary_data$subregions
tot_area <- as.numeric(summary_data$total_area_km2)
n_sites <- as.integer(ledger_data$total_included)
dom_totals <- summary_data$domain_totals

clean_dept_name <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(x)
  s <- gsub("&", "and", s, fixed = TRUE)
  if (identical(s, "Bogota Capital District")) return("Bogotá Capital District")
  if (identical(s, "Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina")) return("San Andrés y Providencia")
  s
}

tot_1835 <- as.numeric(dom_totals[["1835"]])
tot_1912 <- as.numeric(dom_totals[["1912"]])
tot_1950 <- as.numeric(dom_totals[["1950"]])
tot_2018 <- as.numeric(dom_totals[["2018"]])
tot_2024 <- as.numeric(dom_totals[["2024"]])
```

# Abstract

Between the founding of the Republic of Colombia in 1819 and the mid-2020s, the territory of modern Colombia expanded more than thirtyfold from a sparsely settled post-colonial republic into South America's third most populous nation. Across 33 administrative divisions encompassing `r viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 1L)` km² of Andean cordilleras, Caribbean and Pacific lowlands, Orinoco plains and Amazonian rainforest, harmonised demographic benchmarks climb from 1,69M (1.687.110) inhabitants at the 1835 New Granada census to 2,24M in 1851 and 2,95M in 1870, reach 17,48M in 1964 and 30,06M in 1985, register 48,26M (48.258.494) at the 2018 national census and attain 52,70M (52.695.952) in 2024 [@Estadistica2020Censo; @Arias2007Una]. Mean population density rose concurrently from 1,43 inhabitants per km² in 1835 to 44,53 inhabitants per km² in 2024, yet spatial concentration remained extreme: by 2024, Bogotá Capital District (7,93M inhabitants, 2.205 per km²) and tiny Atlántico (2,83M, 609,1 per km²) contrasted sharply with the vast eastern departments of Amazonas, Guainía and Vaupés at 0,8 inhabitants per km². Four structural processes drove this two-century redistribution: late nineteenth-century highland colonisation across the coffee axis (*colonización antioqueña*), mid-twentieth-century rural displacement during *La Violencia* and the post-1960 urban exodus, one of Latin America's swiftest fertility transitions from 6,8 births per woman around 1960 to 1,7 by 2023, and the arrival of Venezuelan migrants after 2017 [@Bacca2013Colonizacion; @Steiner2008Exodos; @Cuervoramirez2025Niveles; @Barbosa2024Estimating]. Unlike primate-city neighbours such as Peru or Argentina, Colombia developed a quadripolar urban system led by Bogotá (7,94M city proper, 9,98M metropolitan area in 2025), Medellín (2,53M proper, 4,19M metro), Santiago de Cali (2,28M proper) and Barranquilla (1,28M proper, 2,29M metro), anchored by a catalogued gazetteer of `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` settlements.

# Background

## Breakup of Gran Colombia and the Early Republican Censuses (1819 to 1870)

Independence from Spain left the northern Andes politically united on paper and demographically fragmented on the ground. Following the victory at Boyacá in 1819 and the Congress of Cúcuta in 1821, the Republic of Colombia (Gran Colombia) joined the former Viceroyalty of New Granada with Venezuela and Quito, attempting to govern a mountainous territory through inherited colonial parish rolls, clerical networks and provincial treasuries [@Ferrari2024Clero]. That federation did not outlast Simón Bolívar's final year: between 1829 and 1830 Venezuela and Ecuador seceded, leaving the central Republic of New Granada confined within borders approximating modern Colombia plus Panama [@Caillavet1997Frontera; @Munoz2006Geografia].

Early republican enumerations revealed how thinly the young state occupied its 1,18M km² landmass. The 1835 census of New Granada recorded 1.687.110 inhabitants across the country, equivalent to barely 1,43 persons per km² (Table \ref{tab:national-benchmarks}). Settlement clung overwhelmingly to cool intermontane basins above 1.500 m along the Eastern and Central Cordilleras, complemented by old colonial ports and river corridors along the Magdalena and Cauca.

Bogotá Capital District and surrounding Cundinamarca together held roughly 322,7k inhabitants in the harmonised 1835 regional allocation, Antioquia held 228,3k, Valle del Cauca 169,9k, Santander 84,8k and Atlántico 83k, while the entire Orinoquia and Amazonia east of the Eastern Cordillera held fewer than 60k enumerated residents.

Under successive nineteenth-century constitutions (the Republic of New Granada, the Granadine Confederation of 1858 and the United States of Colombia of 1863), national censuses in 1851 (2.243.729) and 1870 (2.951.324) charted steady agrarian expansion at 1,45% to 1,80% per annum [@Munoz2006Geografia].

Between 1849 and 1859, Agustín Codazzi's Chorographic Commission mapped the provinces systematically for the first time, exposing the gulf between highland mestizo and criollo elites in Bogotá and the Afro-Colombian, indigenous and mixed coastal and frontier populations of the Caribbean, Chocó and southern Andes [@Munoz2006Geografia; @Cassiani2005Resenas]. Poor mule trails and seasonal Magdalena steamboats kept domestic markets balkanised; even Bogotá shrank temporarily between 1835 (35k) and 1851 (29,6k) amid civil wars and cholera outbreaks before reaching 40,9k in 1870.

## Colonisation of the Coffee Axis and the Separation of Panama (1870 to 1938)

Between 1870 and the Second World War, Colombia shifted its economic and demographic centre of gravity westward along the slopes of the Central Cordillera. Land-hungry peasant families from highland Antioquia moved southward across steep volcanic ridges into southwestern Antioquia, Caldas, Risaralda, Quindío and northern Tolima and Valle del Cauca, clearing forest for maize, cattle and smallholder coffee plantations [@Bacca2013Colonizacion; @Meza1995Resena].

In municipalities such as Jardín, Manizales, Pereira and Armenia, partible family inheritance and secure smallholder titles fostered high rural marital fertility alongside rapid town foundation [@Bacca2013Colonizacion]. By 1938, Manizales had expanded from 10,6k inhabitants in 1870 to 86k, Pereira from 4,8k to 60,5k and Armenia from 13,7k in 1912 to 50,8k, turning the coffee axis into Colombia's densest agrarian belt outside the Sabana de Bogotá.

Political crisis and territorial loss marked the turn of the century. The War of a Thousand Days (1899 to 1902) cost tens of thousands of lives and shattered public finances, culminating in the United States-backed secession of the Department of Panama in November 1903. Loss of the isthmus severed Colombia's direct interoceanic link, yet accelerated completion of the Pacific railway from Cali to Buenaventura in 1915, transforming Valle del Cauca into a booming sugar-cane and commercial corridor [@Meza1995Resena].

Concurrently, Barranquilla overtook older walled Cartagena as Colombia's chief Atlantic entrepôt, climbing from 11,6k in 1870 to 40,1k in 1905, 64,5k in 1918 and 152,3k in 1938 as river steamers and coastal rail lines linked Caribbean trade to the Andean interior [@Lopez2019Demografia].

National statistical administration matured during the same decades. Following irregular counts in 1905 and 1912, the Contraloría General de la República standardised *de facto* enumerations in 1918 and 1938, establishing reliable municipal returns across urban *cabeceras* and rural *veredas* [@Estadistica2020Censo; @Steiner2008Exodos]. By 1938, Bogotá had reached 330,3k residents, Medellín 168,3k, Barranquilla 152,3k and Santiago de Cali 101,9k, signalling the emergence of Colombia's four-city urban industrial core [@Cruz2015Analisis; @Lopez2019Demografia].

## La Violencia, Rural-to-Urban Flight and the DANE Era (1938 to 1985)

The assassination of Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in Bogotá on 9 April 1948 ignited *La Violencia*, a decade of partisan rural terror across Tolima, Caldas, Valle del Cauca, Santander, Boyacá and the eastern Llanos that claimed roughly 200k lives and uprooted hundreds of thousands of peasant households [@Steiner2008Exodos; @Meza1995Resena]. Insecurity in the countryside coincided with import-substitution industrialisation in textiles, food processing and light metallurgy concentrated in Bogotá, Medellín, Cali and Barranquilla [@Lopez2019Demografia; @Cruz2015Analisis]. Millions of smallholders and landless tenants fled toward city peripheries, initiating an unprecedented urban surge [@Steiner2008Exodos].

In 1953, the Colombian state founded the Departamento Administrativo Nacional de Estadística (DANE) to professionalise national censuses after the disrupted 1951 count [@Estadistica2020Censo]. Subsequent DANE enumerations in 1964, 1973 and 1985 documented one of the fastest demographic expansions in modern South American history. Mortality plunged as malaria control, piped urban water, antibiotics and vaccination cut infant deaths, while birth rates remained high until the late 1960s [@Florez1995Transicion; @Arias2007Una]. National population doubled in little over two decades, rising from 17,48M in 1964 to 22,92M in 1973 (at 3,05% annualised growth) and 30,06M in 1985 (Table \ref{tab:national-benchmarks}).

Cities bore the full weight of that natural increase plus rural flight. Bogotá expanded tenfold in three and a half decades, jumping from 330,3k in 1938 to 648,3k in 1951, 1,70M in 1964, 2,57M in 1973 and 3,80M in 1985 [@Hidalgo2015Paro; @Villegas2017Renovacion].

Over the same interval, Medellín grew from 168,3k to 1,45M, Cali from 101,9k to 1,59M and Barranquilla from 152,3k to 833,9k. Because formal housing markets could not absorb tens of thousands of incoming families each year, self-built *barrios de invasión* multiplied across southern Bogotá (notably Ciudad Bolívar), the steep *comunas* of Medellín's Aburrá Valley, eastern Cali (Aguablanca) and secondary Caribbean towns such as Montería and Sincelejo [@Hidalgo2015Paro; @Ocampo2003Urbanizacion; @H2012Procesos].

## Fertility Transition, Internal Displacement and Venezuelan Migration (1985 to 2026)

Few nations experienced as rapid a demographic transition as Colombia between 1965 and 2023. Total fertility fell from approximately 6,8 children per woman in the early 1960s to 4,7 around 1973, 3,2 in 1985, 2,4 by 2005 and 1,7 by 2023, sinking well below the 2,1 replacement floor [@Florez1995Transicion; @Arias2007Una; @Cuervoramirez2025Niveles].

Rising female secondary and university schooling, urban labour-force participation, delayed union formation and widespread contraception compressed birth cohorts across both metropolitan cores and secondary departments [@Archila2022Fecundidad; @Cuervoramirez2025Niveles]. Consequently, annualised national population growth slowed sharply from 2,86% in 1985-1993 to 0,90% in 1993-2005 and 1,09% in 2005-2018, while the median age climbed and older age brackets expanded rapidly [@Castellanos2022Envejecimiento].

Even as natural increase cooled, internal armed conflict between state forces, left-wing guerrillas and right-wing paramilitary blocs displaced millions of rural residents from Chocó, Antioquia, Bolívar, Magdalena, Cesar, Meta, Caquetá and Putumayo between 1990 and 2016 [@Camargo2020Exploring; @Sandoval2014Demographic]. Forced migration pushed urban boundaries onto peri-urban slopes around Popayán, Medellín, Soacha and Cartagena while accelerating agricultural frontier clearing and pasture conversion across the Andean foothills and Amazonian fringe [@Fernandez2013Vereda; @Camargo2020Exploring].

After 2016, the peace accord with the FARC moderated rural violence in several corridors, just as economic collapse in neighbouring Venezuela reversed a half-century of Colombian outward emigration. Between 2017 and 2025, Colombia absorbed roughly 2,8M Venezuelan migrants and returning binational families, lifting the post-2018 national growth rate back to 1,48% per annum and propelling national population from 48,26M in 2018 to 52,70M in 2024 [@Barbosa2024Estimating; @Ospina2023This].

Migrants concentrated overwhelmingly in Bogotá, Medellín, Barranquilla, Cúcuta and intermediate Caribbean and Andean cities, reshaping urban labour markets and household age pyramids across the early 2020s [@Barbosa2024Estimating; @Ospina2023This]. Within Bogotá alone, household survey analyses from 2021 demonstrated high Venezuelan participation in retail, hospitality and construction alongside sharp educational and wage segmentation relative to native workers [@Ospina2023This].

# Methodology

## Territorial Partition across Thirty-Three Sub-Regions

To preserve full spatial continuity across two centuries of republican boundary reforms, Colombia is partitioned into 33 canonical sub-regions corresponding to the 32 modern departments plus Bogotá Capital District, spanning `r viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 1L)` km² (Figure \ref{fig:hero-colombia-map}). Grouping these units into Colombia's five physiographic zones illuminates contrasting ecological constraints [@Estadistica2021Informe; @Caillavet1997Frontera]:

The Andean Highlands and Intermontane Valleys form the historic demographic heartland, uniting Bogotá Capital District (3.596,2 km² in the harmonised mask grid), Cundinamarca (25.154,8 km²), Boyacá (25.457,3 km²), Antioquia (55.658,6 km²), Caldas (8.206,6 km²), Risaralda (5.730,2 km²), Quindío (3.424,4 km²), Santander (26.949,4 km²), Norte de Santander (26.864,6 km²), Tolima (19.871,6 km²) and Huila (23.244,8 km²). Much of this rural settlement remains clustered between 1.000 m and 3.000 m elevation, bordering fragile high-Andean *páramo* ecosystems quantified by DANE at the 2018 census [@Estadistica2021Informe].

The Caribbean Littoral encompasses Atlántico (4.641,3 km²), Bolívar (24.788,4 km²), Córdoba (26.594,7 km²), Magdalena (26.199,6 km²), Cesar (20.578,7 km²), Sucre (14.415,7 km²) and La Guajira (24.153,6 km²). The Pacific Slope and Southwest unite Valle del Cauca (24.074,8 km²), Cauca (26.250,7 km²), Nariño (34.846,3 km²) and humid Chocó (53.013,3 km²). East of the Andes lie the vast Orinoquia Llanos and Amazonian Basin: Meta (81.431,4 km²), Casanare (43.430,6 km²), Arauca (28.322 km²), Vichada (97.199,3 km²), Caquetá (84.390 km²), Putumayo (32.712,1 km²), Guaviare (60.154 km²), Guainía (77.101,4 km²), Vaupés (62.156,3 km²) and Amazonas (111.990,9 km²). Finally, the insular Caribbean department of Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina covers 669,5 km² in the regional grid mask.

## Census Harmonisation, Benchmark Series and Gazetteer Reconciliation

Regional population series are assembled across 13 benchmark years: 1835, 1851, 1870, 1912, 1938, 1950, 1964, 1973, 1985, 1993, 2005, 2018 and 2024. Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century figures draw on the national enumerations of 1835, 1851, 1870, 1912 and 1938, while mid-twentieth-century and modern series integrate the DANE and Contraloría censuses of 1951 (indexed to the 1950 benchmark), 1964, 1973, 1985, 1993, 2005 and 2018 together with DANE's CNPV 2018-calibrated departmental projections to 2024 [@Estadistica2020Censo; @Estadistica2021Informe].

For each sub-region $r$ of area $A_r$ and population $P_r(t)$, spatial density $d_r(t)$ and compound annual intercensal growth $g_r(t_1, t_2)$ follow:

$$d_r(t) = \frac{P_r(t)}{A_r}, \qquad g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Because Colombia created several modern departments only after 1964 - splitting Quindío (1966), Risaralda (1966) and Sucre (1966) from Old Caldas and Bolívar, Cesar (1967) from Magdalena, Casanare (1973) from Boyacá, and raising former *intendencias* and *comisarías* such as Guaviare (1977) to full departmental status under the 1991 Constitution - the regional matrix treats pre-segregation parent counts and modern backfills carefully as documented under Testing and Validation.

Parallel to departmental totals, the settlement gazetteer compiles `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` geocoded places in four ingestion waves tracked by the chapter source ledger. Wave 1 ingested 898 primary records from DANE's 1985-2042 municipal population series and DIVIPOLA registry.

Wave 2 added 157 georeferenced and metro-reconciled records (17,48% gain), Wave 3 added 67 historical nineteenth- and twentieth-century municipal backfill entries (6,35% gain), and Wave 4 closed remaining sub-regional gaps with 5 verified local seats (0,45% marginal gain), leaving zero crowd-sourced fallback entries and zero unaccounted records.

Municipal limits remain unified at city level: Bogotá Capital District is retained as a single municipal core rather than fragmented into its 20 urban *localidades*, while 38 extra-municipal commuter municipalities carry suburb status and four metropolitan aggregates reconcile multi-municipal urban belts [@Vega2016Movilidad; @Barbosa2024Estimating].

# Testing and Validation

## National Benchmark Coherence and Intercensal Growth

Table \ref{tab:national-benchmarks} summarises the 13 national benchmarks from 1835 to 2024, alongside mean terrestrial density, intercensal percentage change and annualised compound growth rates. Across the full 189-year span, Colombia's harmonised population multiplied 31,23 times, climbing from 1,69M in 1835 to 52,70M in 2024 at a long-run compound rate of 1,84% per annum.

```{r tab-national-benchmarks, results='asis'}
yrs_chr <- as.character(unlist(summary_data$benchmark_years))
bench_rows <- vector("list", length(yrs_chr))
for (i in seq_along(yrs_chr)) {
  y <- yrs_chr[i]
  p_cur <- as.numeric(dom_totals[[y]])
  d_cur <- p_cur / tot_area
  if (i == 1L) {
    chg_str <- "-"
    cagr_str <- "-"
  } else {
    y_prev <- yrs_chr[i - 1L]
    p_prev <- as.numeric(dom_totals[[y_prev]])
    dy <- as.integer(y) - as.integer(y_prev)
    pct <- 100 * (p_cur / p_prev - 1)
    cagr <- 100 * ((p_cur / p_prev)^(1 / dy) - 1)
    chg_str <- paste0("+", viscount_fmt_number(pct, 2L), "%")
    cagr_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(cagr, 2L), "%")
  }
  bench_rows[[i]] <- data.frame(
    Year = y,
    Population = viscount_fmt_number(p_cur, 0L),
    Short = viscount_fmt_pop(p_cur),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(d_cur, 2L),
    Change = chg_str,
    CAGR = cagr_str,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}
df_nat <- do.call(rbind, bench_rows)
rownames(df_nat) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_nat,
  "National population benchmarks, mean densities (inhabitants per km²), intercensal gains and compound annual growth rates across Colombia, 1835 to 2024.",
  c("Year", "Total Population", "Short Form", "Density (per km²)", "Intercensal Change", "Annual Growth"),
  list(label = "tab:national-benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Two structural artefacts appear when inspecting the raw regional summation alongside official national census publications. First, in the 1912 (6,56M), 1938 (11,08M) and 1950 (14,37M) columns, the regional matrix sums above the historical contemporary national enumerations (approximately 5,07M in 1912, 8,70M in 1938 and 11,55M in 1951) because both pre-segregation parent departments (such as Cundinamarca, Old Caldas, Bolívar and Magdalena) and their later twentieth-century daughter territories (Bogotá Capital District, Risaralda, Quindío, Sucre and Cesar) carry reconstructed historical totals in the 33-unit grid. Second, in the 1964 benchmark (17,48M total), which closely matches the official 1964 census of 17,48M, unsegregated units not yet separated administratively from parent departments retain minimal placeholder floors (1.313 in Bogotá Capital District while counted within Cundinamarca's 2,82M, 217 in Cesar, 202 in Risaralda, 174 in Sucre, 122 in Quindío and 100 in Casanare and Guaviare) before appearing independently in 1973 and 1985.

## Cross-Checks Against Demographic Transition and Urban Studies

Modern benchmarks from 1985 to 2024 align directly with DANE's reconciled CNPV 2018 series and CEPAL-CELADE demographic evaluations [@Estadistica2020Censo; @Cuervoramirez2025Niveles]. In 2018, DANE counted 44.164.417 persons directly in field interviews and adjusted the final national census population to 48.258.494 after post-enumeration coverage reconciliation across remote rural *veredas* and informal urban peripheries [@Estadistica2020Censo].

The implied intercensal deceleration from 3,05% annual growth in 1964-1973 and 2,86% in 1985-1993 down to 0,90% in 1993-2005 and 1,09% in 2005-2018 matches independent age-structure and fertility reconstructions showing Colombia crossing replacement fertility in the early 2010s before falling to 1,7 births per woman by 2023 [@Arias2007Una; @Castellanos2022Envejecimiento; @Cuervoramirez2025Niveles].

Similarly, the post-2018 uptick to 1,48% annual growth (reaching 52,70M in 2024) accords with DANE and migration studies attributing roughly 2,8M net additions to Venezuelan inflows [@Barbosa2024Estimating; @Ospina2023This]. Within the 2024 demographic profile, urban centres absorbed almost all net cohort expansion while rural highland municipalities continued losing young adults through internal migration [@Steiner2008Exodos; @Castellanos2022Envejecimiento].

# Results

## National Trajectory and Regional Density Contrasts (1835 to 2024)

Colombia's post-independence demographic curve divides cleanly into three regimes: slow nineteenth-century agrarian growth (1,45% to 1,80% per annum from 1835 to 1870), accelerating twentieth-century mortality decline and urbanisation culminating between 1950 and 1993 (peaking at 3,05% per annum in 1964-1973) and mature fertility-driven deceleration punctuated by post-2017 Venezuelan immigration (Figure \ref{fig:colombia-trajectory}).

Between 1950 and 1993 alone, the nation added 23,29M inhabitants, shifting from a predominantly rural society into one where roughly four-fifths of residents dwell in municipal urban *cabeceras* [@Steiner2008Exodos; @Arias2007Una].

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/colombia_after_independence_population_trajectory.png",
  "National and leading departmental demographic trajectories from 1835 to 2024 (Panel A) and top ten sub-regional population densities in 2024 (Panel B).",
  "fig:colombia-trajectory"
)
```

By 2024, sub-regional densities varied across nearly three orders of magnitude (Figure \ref{fig:colombia-trajectory}, Panel B). Bogotá Capital District reached 2.205 inhabitants per km², followed by compact coastal Atlántico at 609,1 per km², industrial-agroindustrial Valle del Cauca at 193 per km² and the three densely settled coffee-axis departments of Risaralda (170), Quindío (165,3) and Caldas (127,5), together with Cundinamarca (141,3) and Antioquia (124).

At the opposite extreme, the three deepest Amazonian departments (Amazonas at 0,77 per km², Vaupés at 0,77 and Guainía at 0,75) and Vichada (1,29) on the Orinoco frontier remained below 1,5 inhabitants per km².

## Departmental Census Totals across Thirty-Three Territories

Table \ref{tab:departmental-censuses} presents the benchmark population series across all 33 sub-regions ranked by their 2024 population, pairing mask area with seven representative historical and modern checkpoints (1835, 1912, 1950, 1973, 1993, 2018 and 2024).

```{r tab-departmental-censuses, results='asis'}
p2024_vec <- vapply(subregions, function(r) as.numeric(r$population[["2024"]]), numeric(1))
ord_sub <- order(p2024_vec, decreasing = TRUE)

dept_rows <- lapply(subregions[ord_sub], function(r) {
  p <- r$population
  data.frame(
    Department = clean_dept_name(r$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(as.numeric(r$area_km2)), 0L),
    P1835 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1835"]]),
    P1912 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1912"]]),
    P1950 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1950"]]),
    P1973 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1973"]]),
    P1993 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1993"]]),
    P2018 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2018"]]),
    P2024 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2024"]]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})

dept_tot <- data.frame(
  Department = "Colombia Total (33 Units)",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(tot_area), 0L),
  P1835 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1835),
  P1912 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1912),
  P1950 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1950),
  P1973 = viscount_fmt_pop(dom_totals[["1973"]]),
  P1993 = viscount_fmt_pop(dom_totals[["1993"]]),
  P2018 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_2018),
  P2024 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_2024),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

df_dept <- rbind(do.call(rbind, dept_rows), dept_tot)
rownames(df_dept) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_dept,
  "Departmental census totals across 33 Colombian territories ranked by 2024 population, 1835 to 2024.",
  c("Territory", "Area (km²)", "1835", "1912", "1950", "1973", "1993", "2018", "2024"),
  list(label = "tab:departmental-censuses", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 36L)
)
```

## Andean Highlands, Coffee Axis and Pacific Rim

The Andean cordilleras and adjacent Pacific valleys continue to anchor Colombia's demographic mass, yet internal growth diverged markedly across sub-regions. Bogotá Capital District and Cundinamarca together rose from 322,7k inhabitants in 1835 to 7,36M in 1993 and 11,48M in 2024 (21,8% of the national total), sustained by capital-city administrative primacy, services and surrounding industrial corridors in Soacha, Chía, Mosquera, Funza and Zipaquirá [@Vega2016Movilidad; @Lopez2019Demografia].

Antioquia expanded 30,24 times from 228,3k in 1835 to 6,90M in 2024, anchored by textile, banking and manufacturing agglomeration in Medellín and the Aburrá Valley alongside twentieth-century banana and cattle colonisation in Urabá [@Jang2015Frecuencia; @Cruz2015Analisis]. In the northeast, Santander (2,38M in 2024) and Norte de Santander (1,71M) maintained dense intermediate networks centred on Bucaramanga and the Venezuelan border crossing at Cúcuta.

By contrast, early demographic heavyweights that lacked large industrial metropolises or experienced sustained out-migration grew far more modestly after 1973. Boyacá climbed from 67,9k in 1835 to 1,05M in 1964 and 1,32M in 1993, then stagnated and dipped to 1,22M in 2018 before recovering modestly to 1,31M in 2024 as highland youths departed for Bogotá [@Steiner2008Exodos].

A similar plateau struck the coffee triad of Caldas (1,05M in 2024), Risaralda (973,9k) and Quindío (566k): after surging through 1964, all three saw sharp fertility declines and emigration following the 1989 collapse of the International Coffee Agreement [@Bacca2013Colonizacion; @Cuervoramirez2025Niveles]. Meanwhile, Valle del Cauca rose from 169,9k in 1835 to 4,65M in 2024 behind Cali, Palmira and Buenaventura [@Meza1995Resena], while Pacific Chocó reached 605,5k (11,4 per km²) and Nariño-Cauca reached 3,28M [@Fernandez2013Vereda].

## Caribbean Littoral, Orinoquia Llanos and Amazonian Frontier

Across northern Colombia, the Caribbean coast expanded steadily in national share after 1950, rising from 2,36M across its seven mainland departments in 1950 to 11,98M in 2024 (22,7% of Colombia's population). Atlántico led every coastal territory in both urban concentration and density, expanding 34,08 times from 83k in 1835 to 2,83M in 2024 behind Barranquilla and neighbouring Soledad [@Lopez2019Demografia].

Bolívar (2,26M, led by Cartagena de Indias), Córdoba (1,91M, led by Montería), Magdalena (1,51M, led by Santa Marta), Cesar (1,40M, led by Valledupar), La Guajira (1,06M) and Sucre (1,01M) combined rapid natural increase during 1950-1993 with agricultural colonisation in the Sinú and Cesar valleys, followed after 2017 by substantial Venezuelan settlement along the northern borderlands [@Ocampo2003Urbanizacion; @Barbosa2024Estimating]. On the insular archipelago of San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina, tourism and commercial free-port status lifted population from 5,7k in 1950 to 61,3k in 2018 and 62,2k in 2024 (93 inhabitants per km²).

East of the Eastern Cordillera, the Orinoquia plains and Amazonian lowlands experienced the steepest relative growth rates of the late twentieth century from tiny nineteenth-century baselines. Meta expanded 43,07 times from 26,6k in 1835 to 1,15M in 2024 as petroleum extraction, cattle ranching and highway links tied Villavicencio directly to Bogotá.

Casanare (475,1k in 2024) and Arauca (317,4k) expanded swiftly on oil booms during the 1980s and 1990s, while Caquetá (428,2k) and Putumayo (388,7k) absorbed displaced Andean colonists into piedmont deforestation fronts [@Camargo2020Exploring; @Caillavet1997Frontera]. Yet the deepest interior territories (Vichada at 125,5k, Guaviare at 100,5k, Amazonas at 86,3k, Guainía at 57,9k and Vaupés at 48k) still accounted collectively for barely 0,79% of Colombia's population across 34,5% of national land area in 2024.

## The Quadripolar Urban System and Metropolitan Growth

Colombia's modern settlement hierarchy exhibits a balanced quadripolar top tier rather than extreme single-city primacy (Figure \ref{fig:colombia-urban-hierarchy}). Across all `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L)` catalogued entries, the rank-size distribution follows a steep Zipfian power law ($\alpha = 1,07$, $R^2 = 0,99$) from million-scale metropolises down to rural municipal seats near 1k inhabitants.

```{r fig-hierarchy, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/colombia_after_independence_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Twelve largest urban and metropolitan entries in Colombia by 2025 population (Panel A) and rank-size power-law fit across 1.127 settlements (Panel B).",
  "fig:colombia-urban-hierarchy"
)
```

In 2025, Bogotá reached 7,94M within its municipal district and 9,98M across its eleven-municipality metropolitan region (anchored by Soacha at 870,1k, Chía at 173,7k, Zipaquirá at 166,8k and Facatativá at 165,2k). Historically, inner-city renewal from Santa Bárbara to the former El Bronx quarter displaced low-income residents outward while rapid peripheral densification strained public transit networks [@Villegas2017Renovacion; @Vanegas2015Antes; @Vega2016Movilidad].

Medellín stood second at 2,53M city proper and 4,19M across the ten municipalities of the Aburrá Valley (including Bello at 601,9k, Itagüí at 304,5k and Envigado at 264,6k) [@H2012Procesos; @Archila2022Fecundidad]. Barranquilla (1,28M proper, 2,29M metropolitan area with Soledad at 722,8k and Malambo at 151,3k) and Santiago de Cali (2,28M proper, flanked by Palmira at 381k, Jamundí at 193,6k, Yumbo at 115,3k and Candelaria at 113,4k) completed the four main poles, followed by Cartagena de Indias (1,01M), Cúcuta (793,2k) and Bucaramanga (617,7k proper, flanked by Floridablanca, Piedecuesta and Girón). Across these urban corridors, recent Venezuelan migration disproportionately reinforced Bogotá, Cúcuta and coastal hubs, altering labour profiles and housing demand [@Barbosa2024Estimating; @Ospina2023This].

# Limitations

Five evidentiary caveats govern interpretation of this demographic reconstruction. First, nineteenth-century enumerations in 1835, 1851 and 1870 under-counted dispersed indigenous populations across Chocó, La Guajira, the Orinoco Llanos and Amazonia, where parish priests and civil commissioners lacked roads or river transport [@Munoz2006Geografia; @Caillavet1997Frontera].

Second, in the 33-unit benchmark matrix, 1912, 1938 and 1950 totals sum above contemporary national census counts (6,56M, 11,08M and 14,37M against roughly 5,07M, 8,70M and 11,55M in published national summaries) because historical estimates for pre-segregation parent departments and post-1966 daughter units coexist in the regional array. Conversely, in 1964, units not yet administratively separated (Bogotá Capital District, Cesar, Risaralda, Quindío, Sucre, Casanare and Guaviare) carry minimal placeholder floors (100 to 1.313) while their actual populations sit inside parent Cundinamarca, Magdalena, Old Caldas, Bolívar and Boyacá.

Third, even modern DANE censuses faced significant coverage challenges during internal armed conflict and rapid informal urbanisation: DANE's 1973 enumeration suffered partial field disruption, while CNPV 2018 required a 4,09M post-enumeration omission adjustment above the 44,16M directly interviewed population [@Estadistica2020Censo].

Fourth, while three metropolitan aggregates (Bogotá, Medellín and Barranquilla) sum core city plus surrounding suburban municipalities, the Cali metropolitan aggregate in the settlement file sums only the four peripheral municipalities (Palmira, Yumbo, Jamundí and Candelaria, 709,4k in 2025) separately from Santiago de Cali (2,28M).

Fifth, post-2018 departmental projections through 2024 incorporate administrative estimates of Venezuelan inflows and rapidly falling post-pandemic fertility that await full verification at Colombia's next decennial census [@Cuervoramirez2025Niveles; @Barbosa2024Estimating].

# Conclusion

Across two centuries from the dissolution of Gran Colombia to 2026, Colombia grew from 1,69M inhabitants in 1835 to 52,70M in 2024, shifting from an isolated constellation of Andean intermontane basins into a metropolitan, service-driven republic. Nineteenth-century highland *colonización antioqueña* and twentieth-century export corridors filled the coffee axis, Valle del Cauca and the Caribbean littoral, before mid-century mortality decline and *La Violencia* triggered an unprecedented rural-to-urban migration.

Unlike neighbours dominated by a single primate capital, Colombia's rugged topography sustained four distinct million-scale urban complexes (Bogotá, Medellín, Cali and Barranquilla) alongside vigorous intermediate centres.

By 2024, one of Latin America's steepest fertility transitions (from 6,8 to 1,7 children per woman) had slowed natural growth and initiated structural ageing, temporarily offset by the arrival of roughly 2,8M Venezuelan migrants who reinforced urban concentration across the Andes and Caribbean rim [@Cuervoramirez2025Niveles; @Castellanos2022Envejecimiento; @Barbosa2024Estimating].

# Appendix

## Macro-Regional Population Shares (1835 to 2024)

Table \ref{tab:macro-regions} aggregates all 33 sub-regions into Colombia's five physiographic macro-regions, highlighting the long-term demographic rise of the Caribbean Littoral and eastern Llanos alongside the persistent predominance of the Andean Highlands.

```{r tab-macro-regions, results='asis'}
macro_map <- list(
  "Andean Highlands" = c("col_bogota_capital_district", "col_cundinamarca", "col_boyaca", "col_antioquia", "col_caldas", "col_risaralda", "col_quindio", "col_santander", "col_norte_de_santander", "col_tolima", "col_huila"),
  "Caribbean Littoral" = c("col_atlantico", "col_bolivar", "col_cordoba", "col_magdalena", "col_cesar", "col_sucre", "col_la_guajira"),
  "Pacific Slope and Southwest" = c("col_valle_del_cauca", "col_cauca", "col_narino", "col_choco"),
  "Orinoquia and Amazonia" = c("col_meta", "col_casanare", "col_arauca", "col_vichada", "col_caqueta", "col_putumayo", "col_guaviare", "col_guainia", "col_vaupes", "col_amazonas"),
  "Insular Caribbean" = c("col_archipielago_de_san_andres_providencia_y_santa_catalina")
)

sub_by_id <- setNames(subregions, vapply(subregions, function(r) r$id, character(1)))

m_rows <- lapply(names(macro_map), function(m_name) {
  ids <- macro_map[[m_name]]
  area_m <- sum(vapply(ids, function(id) as.numeric(sub_by_id[[id]]$area_km2), numeric(1)))
  p35 <- sum(vapply(ids, function(id) as.numeric(sub_by_id[[id]]$population[["1835"]]), numeric(1)))
  p12 <- sum(vapply(ids, function(id) as.numeric(sub_by_id[[id]]$population[["1912"]]), numeric(1)))
  p50 <- sum(vapply(ids, function(id) as.numeric(sub_by_id[[id]]$population[["1950"]]), numeric(1)))
  p93 <- sum(vapply(ids, function(id) as.numeric(sub_by_id[[id]]$population[["1993"]]), numeric(1)))
  p18 <- sum(vapply(ids, function(id) as.numeric(sub_by_id[[id]]$population[["2018"]]), numeric(1)))
  p24 <- sum(vapply(ids, function(id) as.numeric(sub_by_id[[id]]$population[["2024"]]), numeric(1)))
  sh24 <- 100 * p24 / tot_2024
  data.frame(
    MacroRegion = m_name,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(area_m), 0L),
    P1835 = viscount_fmt_pop(p35),
    P1912 = viscount_fmt_pop(p12),
    P1950 = viscount_fmt_pop(p50),
    P1993 = viscount_fmt_pop(p93),
    P2018 = viscount_fmt_pop(p18),
    P2024 = viscount_fmt_pop(p24),
    Share24 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(sh24, 1L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_macro <- do.call(rbind, m_rows)
rownames(df_macro) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_macro,
  "Macro-regional population totals and 2024 national shares across five physiographic zones of Colombia, 1835 to 2024.",
  c("Macro-Region", "Area (km²)", "1835", "1912", "1950", "1993", "2018", "2024", "2024 Share"),
  list(label = "tab:macro-regions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
